prompt: Why does running a k6 script need no Node.js and no `npm install`?
hint: What kind of program is k6?

choices.text: k6 downloads Node.js the first time a script is run
choices.why: Nothing is downloaded; the one file from the archive is the whole tool.

choices.text: The scripts are compiled to Go before k6 runs them
choices.why: The JavaScript is interpreted inside k6; it is not translated into Go source.

choices.text: k6 is one Go program with a JavaScript engine of its own inside
choices.why: Right. The script runs inside k6 itself, so the archive's single file is everything.

choices.text: Ubuntu 24.04 ships a JavaScript runtime in its base
choices.why: The base packages of lesson 1 hold no JavaScript runtime, and k6 would not use one.

prompt: Five looping virtual users each send one request and then sleep for 1 s. If every answer took 250 ms, how many requests a second would the five of them send in total?
hint: One iteration lasts the answer plus the sleep.

prompt: What does `-q` change in `k6 run -q k6/first.js`?
hint: Compare a run with and without it.

choices.text: It hides the logo and the progress line that k6 redraws while it runs
choices.why: Right. The end-of-test summary is the same with and without it.

choices.text: It shortens the summary to the thresholds and the checks, leaving out the rest
choices.why: The summary keeps every line; only what is printed during the run goes.

choices.text: It turns off the checks to make the run quicker
choices.why: Checks run as usual; `-q` is about the terminal, not the test.

choices.text: It runs the test in the background
choices.why: The command still holds the terminal until the test ends.

prompt: A colleague puts `const shows = http.get(BASE + '/shows').json();` at the top level of the script, outside every function. What happens when the script is run?

choices.text: It is sent once per iteration and counted in `http_reqs`
choices.why: That would be the default function. The top level is init code.

choices.text: k6 stops with an error before any load, and exits with 107
choices.why: Right. Init code may not send requests; data needed before the load belongs in setup().

choices.text: It is sent once, by the first virtual user, and its answer is shared by all
choices.why: Init code runs for every virtual user, and in any case k6 refuses a request there.

choices.text: It is sent by each virtual user before the load, and left out of the summary
choices.why: A reasonable guess about init code, but k6 refuses the request instead of sending it.

prompt: Why does the script add 409 to the expected statuses with `http.setResponseCallback`?
hint: What does a 409 mean at the box office?

choices.text: A 409 is the seat being taken, a correct answer, and should not count as failed
choices.why: Right. Left out, every refused seat would raise `http_req_failed` though nothing went wrong.

choices.text: So that k6 retries the booking with another seat
choices.why: k6 does not retry; the callback only decides what counts as a failure.

choices.text: To make the 409 answers faster
choices.why: The callback changes how answers are counted, not how the server answers.

choices.text: Because k6 treats a 4xx answer as a crash of the script and stops the test
choices.why: k6 counts an unexpected status in `http_req_failed` and carries on.

prompt: Match each piece of a k6 scenario to what it decides.

pairs.right: a fixed number of users, each looping as soon as it finishes
one rate of new iterations a second, held for a duration
a rate of new iterations that moves through stages
how many users k6 may have busy before it drops iterations

right_distractors: how many times a failed request is retried

prompt: The box office starts answering `GET /shows/{id}` with a 200 whose body has no `left` field. With the script as written, what does the run report?
hint: Which of the two mechanisms is watching the body?

choices.text: `http_req_failed` rises above 1%, so the run ends with exit code 99
choices.why: The status is 200, an expected one, so no request counts as failed.

choices.text: A cross on `seats left is a number`, and the run exits 0
choices.why: Right. A check counts the failure, and no threshold watches the checks.

choices.text: k6 stops the scenario at the first wrong body and exits with 107
choices.why: A check never stops anything; it is counted and the iteration carries on.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: The check does see it: it prints a cross with the count of failures.

prompt: In the threshold key `http_req_duration{name:booking}`, the part in braces keeps only the requests carrying that ___.
hint: Set with `tags:` in the request's parameters.

prompt: Why does the browse request carry `tags: { name: 'show' }` when its address already says which show it asks for?

choices.text: Without a tag k6 leaves the request out of the summary and of every threshold
choices.why: Untagged requests are counted like any other, under their address.

choices.text: The tag sends the name to the server as a header
choices.why: Tags stay inside k6; the server never sees them.

choices.text: It names the step of the journey for whoever reads the script in a code review
choices.why: `group('browse', …)` already does that; the tag has a job in the metrics.

choices.text: The twenty addresses then count as one request for metrics and thresholds
choices.why: Right. One name groups `/shows/981` to `/shows/1000` into one line instead of twenty.

prompt: `k6 run` ends with `exit 99`. What does that code say?

choices.text: The script has a syntax error
choices.why: An error in the script stops k6 before the load, with another code: 107 in this lesson.

choices.text: At least one threshold was crossed
choices.why: Right. 99 is k6's code for crossed thresholds, whatever the other lines say.

choices.text: A check failed in more than 1% of iterations
choices.why: Checks do not set the exit code unless a threshold watches them.

choices.text: The server stopped answering halfway
choices.why: Refused connections would show in `http_req_failed`; 99 is about thresholds.

prompt: In the run at 30 journeys a second, `http_req_failed` was 0.00% and all 801 checks passed, yet the run failed. Why?
hint: What did the box office do with each request?

choices.text: k6 counted the 409 answers as failures after all
choices.why: Then `http_req_failed` would not be 0.00%.

choices.text: Every answer was correct and late, and the time thresholds were crossed
choices.why: Right. Slow is not an error, which is why the requirement carries a time threshold as well.

choices.text: The 260 dropped iterations are counted as failed requests by the threshold
choices.why: A dropped iteration sends nothing, so it adds no request to any metric of requests.

choices.text: Checks that pass make k6 exit 99
choices.why: Passing checks do nothing to the exit code.

prompt: The summary of an arrival-rate run shows `dropped_iterations: 260`. What should you conclude before reading any percentile?
hint: Who starts an iteration in that executor?

choices.text: 260 requests failed and are left out of `http_req_failed`
choices.why: Dropped iterations never sent a request, so there was nothing to fail.

choices.text: The server refused 260 connections
choices.why: The drops happen inside k6, which had no free virtual user to start them with.

choices.text: The run applied less load than it was written for
choices.why: Right. k6 ran out of virtual users, so the percentiles describe a lighter test.

choices.text: 260 iterations were retried after a timeout
choices.why: k6 retries nothing; a dropped iteration simply never starts.

prompt: Which of these make `k6 run` end with a non-zero exit code? Choose every one that applies.
hint: Which mechanisms decide the exit code?

choices.text: The 95th percentile of `http_req_duration` passes the limit in `thresholds`
choices.why: Right. A crossed threshold is the exit code 99.

choices.text: `checks: ['rate>0.99']` is in `thresholds`, and 5% of checks fail
choices.why: Right. With a threshold on them, failed checks decide the result.

choices.text: A check fails in 5% of iterations and no threshold mentions checks
choices.why: Without a threshold, a failed check is a count in the summary and the exit code stays 0.

choices.text: Some bookings answer 409, which the response callback lists as expected
choices.why: An expected status is a success, so it moves no metric of failure.

prompt: Why does the summary print a `{ name:booking }` line under `http_req_duration` but none for `{ name:show }`?

choices.text: Only POST requests get a line of their own
choices.why: The method has nothing to do with it; a threshold does.

choices.text: A threshold names `name:booking`, and none names `name:show`
choices.why: Right. k6 prints a tag's line when a threshold asks about it.

choices.text: The show requests were too fast to measure apart
choices.why: They were measured; nobody asked for them apart.

choices.text: Groups hide the tags of the requests inside them
choices.why: Groups and tags are separate, and the full summary shows both.

prompt: Put the phases of one request over an open connection in the order they happen, as the full summary names them.
A new requirement reads: "checkout completes within 2 s at the 95th percentile at 20 orders a second". Which scenario tests it as written?
hint: Is the load a number of people or a rate?

choices.text: `constant-vus` with 20 users, each sleeping one second between requests
choices.why: That is about 20 a second only while answers are instant; as they slow, the rate falls.

choices.text: `constant-arrival-rate` at 20 a second, with enough `maxVUs` that none is dropped
choices.why: Right. The requirement is a rate, and an arrival rate holds it however slow the answers get.

choices.text: `ramping-arrival-rate` from 1 to 200 a second
choices.why: That looks for the breaking point; the requirement names one load to hold.

choices.text: `constant-vus` with 20 users and no sleep
choices.why: Each user waits for its answer, so the rate depends on the server, not on the requirement.

prompt: A run with `vus: 50` and `duration: '10m'` passes its `p(95)<200` threshold. The summary also shows `http_reqs` at 12 a second, where the team expected about 40. What is the most likely reading?
hint: Who sets the pace with looping virtual users?

choices.text: The test is valid, since the threshold is what decides
choices.why: The threshold held at a load nobody asked for, so the verdict answers a different question.

choices.text: k6 is too slow to send 40 requests a second
choices.why: k6 sent what its users asked for; each user was waiting on the server.

choices.text: The answers slowed down, the looping users sent fewer requests, and the test eased off
choices.why: Right. The closed loop lowered the load, and the percentile describes the lighter test.

choices.text: Half the requests failed and were left out of `http_reqs`
choices.why: Failed requests are still counted in `http_reqs`.

prompt: A pipeline step runs `k6 run -q load.js` and the job stays green although the team knows the error rate went up to 30%. The script asserts every response with `check`, and its only entry under `thresholds` is `http_req_duration: ['p(95)<500']`. What is missing?
hint: What fails the run when requests fail fast?

choices.text: The `-q` flag, which hides the failures from the pipeline
choices.why: `-q` hides only the progress bar; the exit code is the same.

choices.text: A threshold on `http_req_failed` or on `checks`
choices.why: Right. Fast errors keep the duration low, and checks alone never set the exit code.

choices.text: A `group` around each request
choices.why: Groups organise the summary and decide nothing.

choices.text: A `sleep` in the default function
choices.why: Think time changes the load, not what counts as a failure.
